title: Is Depression An Immune-Mediated Disease?
subtitle: A new study uses white blood cell measurements to predict response in rTMS treatment.
body_html:
The Frontier Psychiatrists is a daily-enough health-themed newsletter. One idea I've been mulling over for a while is the connection between immune function and psychiatric symptoms.

I see a lot of patients who end up having immunological disorders or autoimmune diseases, and I have a confirmed track record of accurate referrals to rheumatology that I'm inordinately proud of. I first got interested in this topic thanks to some work I did on a series of review papers I senior authored with my friends, especially first author Burton Tabaac, M.D., related to psychedelic medicines. In our paper on psilocybin, we highlight its role as a plausible anti-inflammatory agent:

It has been well-established that inflammation is associated with psychiatric disorders, with biochemical markers of inflammation noted in psychiatric populations. However, the direction of causality between inflammation and psychiatric symptom is not clear. Increased inflammation as a side effect of medical care has been linked to suicidality. Conversely, anti-inflammatory agents have been explored as treatments for depression. Of note, a “mega-analysis” of 18 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) found that immunomodulatory drugs targeting a range of mechanisms caused a modest but significant decrease in core depressive symptoms. Animal models have observed a correlation between reduced inflammation and decreases in addictive behaviors. Taken together, these data suggest that a reduction of inflammation may contribute to perceived wellness and reduced psychopathology.1

It sure seems like I already thinks inflammation plays a role in depression? Today, looking for what to write about, I found a paper that grabbed my attention:

Higher neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio predicts poor response to repetetive transcranial magnetic stimulation(rTMS) in treatment-resistant depression

Wait a minute—as a doctor who prescribes rTMS, having a sense of who will benefit and, who will not, seems… important. To my grammar and spelling enthusiast readers—that is a copy-pasta from a journal article title. I didn’t simply misspell repetitive. It’s spelled differently in other parts of the world!

For general audiences, some background is in order: Neutrophils and lymphocytes are both white blood cells. These two different kinds of white blood cells handle different parts of our immune response.

This is a retrospective study. That means it's hypothesis-generating, not that it can prove a hypothesis. In the sample, they looked at patients who were treated with rTMS for depression and then went back and reviewed their blood work.

We retrospectively reviewed 86 patients with TRD who received 10 Hz rTMS to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) at Gazi University between June 2017 and June 2023. Inflammatory markers, including neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), and systemic immune-inflammatory index (SII), were evaluated.2

One of the dangers of this kind of research is that it's vulnerable to a phenomenon we call P-hacking. Essentially, if you have a bunch of statistical comparisons you can make, and you don't have a hypothesis specified in advance, you can run a series of comparisons, and then publish the one that turns out to be “significant.” there is some theoretical protection against cherry picking statistically, significant results based on an arbitrary cut off using math, called the Bonferoni correction. With that statistical caveat aside, let's dig into why they thought about looking at rTMS outcomes and inflammatory markers in the first place. I’m not saying the findings we will look at next are P-hacked. I am saying replication is important, no matter how exciting the finding is.

As the authors point out, in depression, inflammation has been implicated for quite some time:

inflammatory dysregulation is a significant factor in the pathogenesis of major depression, as demonstrated by both preclinical and clinical researches [9, 10]. Numerous studies have indicated that elevated levels of inflammatory markers are linked to the severity of depression and resistance to treatment [11]. Meta-analyzes on the connection between inflammatory mediators in depression often focus on proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, C-reactive protein (CRP) and anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 [12,13,14,15].

When we say inflammation, it’s easy to assume people know what it means. For a hot minute, (GET IT?) I'm not going to make that assumption. I will explain what inflammation is.

Share

The immune system has both specific defenses—the learning immune system, those lymphocytes, and antibodies that learn to recognize dangerous pathogens in the environment and be prepared the next time they present themselves to kill them. This is where vaccination plays a role—teaching the immune system to be on the lookout for something that could infect you well before it does so is useful. There are many nonspecific immune defenses, too. These include your skin, which keeps infectious agents out. Their other non-specific immune responses “blow up” anything likely to cause a problem for your body. That's where neutrophils come in. Neutrophils are causing inflammation broadly because they're doing chemical warfare inside your body. If you think of soap or bleach, those are external nonspecific immunologic “defenses” we use to clean up our environment. Between bleach and soap, you can disinfect almost anything. Now, there are some particular pathogens you can't successfully disinfect that way, and in the hospital, we use an autoclave—an oven to bake the pathogen to the point it's dead.

If you think of inflammation as an autoclave in your own body or your internal bleach supply, you're getting it right. When you get a fever? That's your body increasing the temperature to kill pathogens. It works. Remember the malaria cure for insanity? I wrote about it about a year ago, and a few few times since, it was the first Nobel prize winning intervention in psychiatry! It was a treatment of giving people malaria so they'd get a temperature of 105—because at 105° temperature would kill their syphilis.

That was an immunologic treatment for a pathogen. Our bodies’ immune response? It can be nonspecific—dumping bleach into our bloodstream. As a process, that doesn't only kill pathogens. It kills a little bit of us every time. The particular immunity of lymphocytes, which is targeted, is much less dangerous to the rest of our body when it’s functioning correctly. It's like a “trained sniper,” only taking out the dangerous invader while avoiding causing any damage to anyone nearby. Inflammation is broad spectrum, so our body gets slightly injured while the pathogens get destroyed.

This nonspecific inflammation? That's what we're worried about when it comes to most psychiatric illnesses. Your body is dumping out “bleach” inside you.

By the way, this is only barely a metaphor. It's not commercial bleach, but the chemical used by neutrophils is an acid, Hypochlorous Acid (HOCl), the same acid as in bleach. There are additional steps to mitigate the risk, but inflammation can harm our bodies. It does so while protecting us from things that could kill us via infectious agents.

When the study's authors looked at the ratio of neutrophils and lymphocytes, they looked at a ratio of nonspecific specific immune activity. As the authors point out, this is easy to measure:

The quantification of neutrophils, platelets, and lymphocytes in peripheral blood, along with their respective ratios such as neutrophil/lymphocyte ratio(NLR), platelet/lymhocyte ratio (PLR), systemic immun inflammatory index (SII) represents cost-effective and straightforward methods for assessing systemic inflammation [18].

Higher ratios of neutrophils? That is increased inflammation. That inflammation has been hypothesized to lead to more depression. In this case, they wanted to look at people who had responded to rTMS versus people who hadn't and check if the amount of inflammation in their body was a predictor of non-response to the treatment. It's possible, for example, that there is inflammatory depression as a subtype that might be relevant for whether someone will respond to transcranial magnetic stimulation as delivered in this setting—which, by the way, was in Ankara, Turkey, at Gazi University Faculty of Medicine Department of Psychiatry. They had a rather large sample to review the data on:

272 patients who met the criteria for major depression and received standard clinical treatment of 10 Hz rTMS to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC)

They have some possible bias in the sample— the retrospective analysis only included those on whom they had complete data, thus excluding those “lost to follow up.” I feel, as readers, this is understandable, as the point of this retrospective review is to be hypothesis generating and includes enough patients to allow for that:

Patients aged 18 and above, who underwent a complete blood count before the 14-day period preceding rTMS treatment, received a minimum of 20 sessions of rTMS over a four-week, and had complete pre- and post-treatment symptom severity scales (Montgomery-Asberg Depression Rating Scale) were included to study.

They note the individuals who were omitted, which wisely excluded those with active infection or other confounding data:

A total of 128 patients who had bipolar depressive disorder or/and co-existing psychiatric disorder (except for smoking addiction), 5 patients who were found to have lymphopenia, and 4 patients who had an active infection during rTMS treatment were not included to the study. 49 patients who had not completed at least 20 sessions of rTMS treatment were also excluded from the study. Patients with diabetes, chronic smoking, hypertension, and known inflammatory diseases were not excluded from the study and recorded to data form.

What they found in the 86 patients who remained is tantalizing! There is a very high correlation between high inflammation as measured by that ratio, the “NLR,” and non-response to rTMS treatment:

This NLR ratio was a powerful explanation of a large portion of the variance in outcomes:

The odds ratio…for NLR was found to be 0.373 (95% CI: 0.161–0.865, p = 0.022). This indicates that an increase in NLR is associated with a decreased likelihood of responding to rTMS. Specifically, for each unit increase in NLR, the odds of a positive response to rTMS decrease by approximately 62.7% (1–0.373), assuming all other variables are held constant.

To give you a point of comparison, the odd ratio contribution of a stressful life event leading to depression is on the order of:

The odds ratio for onset of major depression in the month of a stressful life event was 5.64 in all subjects,

And without boring you with some extremely dull math, that odds ratio can be converted into an explanation of a percentage of the variance explained. NLR is responsible for approximately 18.7% of the variance in the outcome variable (onset of depression) when looking at stressful life events. This is a substantial effect size.3

Comparing apples to apples, with a bit more math hidden in the background, this study’s finding, with its odds ratio of 0.373, accounts for approximately 7.0% of the variance in the likelihood of response to rTMS.

It's more of a big predictor than the response in the first week to once-daily TMS, at least in their sample:

It's not a trivial order of magnitude. This is potentially a big-deal finding, and it should be replicated—which I'm writing this article to suggest somebody do.

So there we have it—a plausible immune biomarker to predict response to a treatment directed at the brain rather than the immune system. It's like living in the future.

Strong work, Dr. Koporal, et. al.!

2

3
